feedback: If the learner cannot name why a wrong card is wrong, re-read both decimals in place-value words and point to where the comparison first decides (the highest differing place).
Praise explicit self-monitoring ('I nearly counted the digits — but I compared tenths first').
If the learner only identifies the right answer without naming the faulty rule, prompt: which rule would make someone pick the wrong card here?
activities.intendedInsight: The error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge; naming the misconception and inspecting clearly-labelled correct/incorrect examples side by side helps a learner catch and override it.
learnerActions: Look at side-by-side comparison cards, one clearly labelled correct and one clearly labelled wrong, e.g. '0.45 > 0.5' (labelled wrong) beside '0.45 < 0.5' (labelled correct).
Say out loud which faulty rule produced the wrong card ('longer-is-larger: it counted 45 against 5') and explain why it fails here.
Write or state the place-value reason the correct card holds (0.5 is 5 tenths; 0.45 is 4 tenths 5 hundredths; 5 tenths is more).
Before answering each new pair, flag the rule you must NOT use, then compare correctly.
activities.title: Name and resist the whole-number rule (correct vs incorrect cards)

feedback: If the learner thinks 0.38 covers more than 0.4 because '38 > 4', count tenths columns: 0.4 fills four full columns (40 squares), 0.38 fills three columns and part of a fourth (38 squares).
If the learner denies 0.7 = 0.70, overlay or count: 7 tenths = 70 hundredths cover the same squares.
On the aligned chart, if the learner compares from the right, redirect to the highest place first.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals can be compared by area as well as by length, and both representations show that annexing a zero (0.7 = 0.70) preserves value while more digits need not mean more size. (Note: the source synthesis treats length as the clearest magnitude model for this topic; the grid is a complementary reference.)
learnerActions: Shade 0.4 and 0.38 each on a 10×10 hundredths grid and compare the shaded areas.
Shade 0.7 on one grid and 0.70 on another, and explain why seven tenths fills the same area as seventy hundredths.
Use an aligned place-value chart (points lined up) to read each decimal digit by digit, starting from tenths, and state which decimal is larger and why.
activities.title: Show equivalence and area with hundredths grids
